newsitem.title: GERMANY: Race to put Dietrich on map hots up in Berlin.
newsitem.headline: Race to put Dietrich on map hots up in Berlin.

text.p: Two Berlin districts began a race on Thursday to put Marlene Dietrich's name on the map, despite some residents' resentment over her support for the Allied cause during World War Two.
The city-centre Tiergarten district threw down the gauntlet by announcing plans to name a new square after Dietrich.
That decision drew a sharp reponse from the Schoeneberg part of the city, where the legendary singer was born and buried.
Schoeneberg councillor Hanns Leske called on Tiergarten to withdraw its plans, vowing his area would agree to name a square after Dietrich before the rival proposal could be approved.

"Tiergarten shooting from the hip like this represents an unfriendly act against Schoeneberg," said Leske, who described the rival move as "a sad and above all unnecessary continuation of a provincial farce" revolving around the film star.
Schoeneberg councillors have long said they want to name a location after Dietrich but failed to agree on a concrete plan.
"The race has now been opened," Schoeneberg mayor Elisabeth Ziemer said. "If the people of Schoeneberg want to do this, they have to decide now. Otherwise the chance will be lost."

The new development marked a turnaround in the debate about whether to honour Dietrich, whom some Berliners regard as a traitor because she quit Germany, became an American citizen and entertained Allied troops during the war.

While Schoeneberg councillors said they wanted to name a street or square after the star of "The Blue Angel", their failure to agree which name should be dropped to make way for her showed the ambivalence of some residents' feelings.

Horst Porath, Tiergarten's top planning official, said he planned to use Dietrich's name for a square being built as part of the Potsdamer Platz area, which will be home to a film museum and 3-D cinema.
"I thought this new location, which is also intended to have great cultural significance, would be a good and appropriate place for Marlene Dietrich," Porath said.

Local planning rules stipulate that once a name has been used claimed by one part of the city, it cannot be used again. As Schoeneberg's next council meeting falls a few days before Tiergarten's, it could still claim the name for itself.
Dietrich arrived in Hollywood in 1930 and took up U.S. citizenship in 1939 at the height of her career. A recluse in her later years, she died in Paris in 1992.

"I think it would be nice if Marlene Dietrich were to get a square in the area where she was born and where she is buried," Ziemer said. But she said the Potsdamer Platz location was an appropriate alternative if her councillors failed to act.

The Potsdamer Platz used to be one the liveliest parts of Berlin, a crossroads between East and West because of a nearby major rail station, but it was destroyed by Allied bombing and lay derelict in the no man's land around the Berlin Wall.

Other likely candidates for a street name in the area include the late Herbert von Karajan, acclaimed conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic, the fairy-tale-telling Brothers Grimm and General Ludwig Beck, a wartime army officer who opposed Hitler.
The new quarter is planned as a glittering mix of high-class hotels, banks, company headquarters and a German Film Museum, which will also house a collection of Dietrich memorabilia.
